power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Gender-Inclusive Voice and Communication Training: Supporting Nonbinary Clients

author.affiliation:
Department of Communicative Sciences and Disorders
								Michigan State University (East Lansing
								
									MI

Department of Communicative Sciences and Disorders
								Michigan State University (East Lansing
								
									MI
									USA

text.text: Nonbinary clients may pursue gender-affirming voice training (GAVT) goals that extend beyond traditional masculinization and feminization goals.

This clinical perspective discusses potential applications of existing clinical frameworks for nonbinary clients, with particular focus on meta-therapy and the Acoustic Assumptions (AA) as gender-inclusive approaches.
These approaches support gender-inclusive, person-centered exploration of voice and communication characteristics while drawing on established principles of speech production.

Although further research is needed to establish more gender-inclusive acoustic and perceptual outcome measures, clinicians can presently use customizable, person-centered approaches to support diverse GAVT goals and provide affirming care.

Despite growing recognition of voice and communicationrelated goals within the transgender and gender diverse (TGD) community, reported acoustic and perceptual outcomes remain largely centered around masculinization or feminization. 1, 2 Implementing this conceptualization in clinical practice may not sufficiently address the genderaffirming voice training (GAVT) goals of nonbinary clients.
text.formatted: Despite growing recognition of voice and communicationrelated goals within the transgender and gender diverse (TGD) community, reported acoustic and perceptual outcomes remain largely centered around masculinization or feminization. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> Implementing this conceptualization in clinical practice may not sufficiently address the genderaffirming voice training (GAVT) goals of nonbinary clients.

text.text: Approaches such as meta-therapy 3 and the Acoustic Assumptions (AA) 4 are theory-grounded, gender-inclusive approaches applicable for use with nonbinary clients.
text.formatted: Approaches such as meta-therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> and the Acoustic Assumptions (AA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> are theory-grounded, gender-inclusive approaches applicable for use with nonbinary clients.

text.text: GAVT may involve adjusting a client's resonance, articulation, respiration, or other components of speech production (e.g., prosody) to achieve their desired voice and communication style. 5 Lev and colleagues 6 define gender-affirming approaches as "...non-pathologizing clinical approaches that embrace diverse gender-related identities, expressions, and experiences as normative and healthy expressions of self," while recognizing how power and privilege influence the therapeutic relationship. 6(p. 24) Regardless of communicative skills, voice-gender incongruence significantly impacts communication experiences for nonbinary people. 7, 8 In supporting clients, clinicians must navigate GAVT service provision with intentional humility toward intersecting experiences of race, gender, or other characteristics that express identity (e.g., indigeneity) to cultivate an affirming space for clients. [9] [10] [11] [12]
text.formatted: GAVT may involve adjusting a client's resonance, articulation, respiration, or other components of speech production (e.g., prosody) to achieve their desired voice and communication style. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> Lev and colleagues <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> define gender-affirming approaches as "...non-pathologizing clinical approaches that embrace diverse gender-related identities, expressions, and experiences as normative and healthy expressions of self," while recognizing how power and privilege influence the therapeutic relationship. <ref type="bibr">6(p. 24)</ref> Regardless of communicative skills, voice-gender incongruence significantly impacts communication experiences for nonbinary people. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> In supporting clients, clinicians must navigate GAVT service provision with intentional humility toward intersecting experiences of race, gender, or other characteristics that express identity (e.g., indigeneity) to cultivate an affirming space for clients. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[12]</ref>

text.text: The World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH) provides empirical support and ethical guidance for gender-affirming healthcare services, including GAVT. 13 The WPATH Standards of Care (8th edition) note that clinicians, "...benefit from avoiding assumptions about how each client conceptualizes their gender and by being prepared to be led by a given client's personal understanding of gender as it relates to the client's gender identity, expression, and any need for medical care." 13(p. 81) Aligning with the WPATH standards and related recommendations for clinician-client communication, 14 clinicians should use open-ended, judgement-free, and identity-affirming interviewing approaches to explore the interplay between identity and GAVT goals.
text.formatted: The World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH) provides empirical support and ethical guidance for gender-affirming healthcare services, including GAVT. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">13</ref> The WPATH Standards of Care (8th edition) note that clinicians, "...benefit from avoiding assumptions about how each client conceptualizes their gender and by being prepared to be led by a given client's personal understanding of gender as it relates to the client's gender identity, expression, and any need for medical care." <ref type="bibr">13(p. 81)</ref> Aligning with the WPATH standards and related recommendations for clinician-client communication, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14</ref> clinicians should use open-ended, judgement-free, and identity-affirming interviewing approaches to explore the interplay between identity and GAVT goals.

text.text: A clinician using an evidence-based approach may take the following steps: 1.
Introduce themself with full name, discipline, and pronouns (e.g., "My name is 2.

Ask a client to share pronouns and name they use, then ask them to describe their gender identity and gender expression goals in their own words (e.g., "How would you describe your gender identity, how you'd like your ideal voice to sound, and how you'd like others to perceive you based on your voice?").
Ask the client to describe their present communication experiences (self-perceptions, other listener perceptions, at home, in the community, etc.).
Ask clients to describe their ideal voice/communication style in their own words.
Invite them to share audio/video examples of characteristics they would (or would not) like to incorporate.
When working with nonbinary clients, above all, clinicians must cultivate a safe, affirming space for clients to describe themselves and their goals in their own words.
Established acoustic theories broadly underlying human speech production, such as source-filter theory, 15 offer theoretical support for gender-inclusive GAVT approaches.
text.formatted: Established acoustic theories broadly underlying human speech production, such as source-filter theory, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> offer theoretical support for gender-inclusive GAVT approaches.

text.text: Source filter theory, a widely accepted theory underpinning human speech production, describes how interactions between the source (i.e., vocal folds) and filter (e.g., tongue, lips) shape acoustic output during speech.

For example, in North American English, the high front vowel /i/ (e.g., heat) has a low F1 and high F2, reflecting the high and forward tongue positioning used to produce this vowel sound. [15] [16] [17] Despite interpersonal variations, 1 these phenomena are generally observed across speakers. 15, 17, 18 Source-filter theory informs GAVT approaches, transcending population demographics (e.g., age, sex, gender) and offering a gender-inclusive explanation of speech production.
text.formatted: For example, in North American English, the high front vowel /i/ (e.g., heat) has a low F1 and high F2, reflecting the high and forward tongue positioning used to produce this vowel sound. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[17]</ref> Despite interpersonal variations, 1 these phenomena are generally observed across speakers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">18</ref> Source-filter theory informs GAVT approaches, transcending population demographics (e.g., age, sex, gender) and offering a gender-inclusive explanation of speech production.

text.text: Listener perceptions of gender are commonly influenced by fundamental frequency (f 0 ), resonance, articulation, and prosody. 2 Acoustically, f 0 correlates with perceived pitch, while formant frequencies index listener perceptions of vocal tract configurations. 15, 16 These are two of the most commonly addressed aspects of speech production addressed in GAVT, in part due to their influence of listener perceptions of gender. 2, 15, 16 Ideally, clinicians should consider all verbal and nonverbal factors influencing communication to comprehensively address a client's goals.
text.formatted: Listener perceptions of gender are commonly influenced by fundamental frequency (f 0 ), resonance, articulation, and prosody. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> Acoustically, f 0 correlates with perceived pitch, while formant frequencies index listener perceptions of vocal tract configurations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16</ref> These are two of the most commonly addressed aspects of speech production addressed in GAVT, in part due to their influence of listener perceptions of gender. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">16</ref> Ideally, clinicians should consider all verbal and nonverbal factors influencing communication to comprehensively address a client's goals.

text.text: To date, GAVT studies have predominantly focused on binary intervention outcomes. 1 However, source-filter theory provides support for gender-inclusive approaches to GAVT, enabling a more comprehensive consideration of the potential goals of nonbinary clients.
text.formatted: To date, GAVT studies have predominantly focused on binary intervention outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> However, source-filter theory provides support for gender-inclusive approaches to GAVT, enabling a more comprehensive consideration of the potential goals of nonbinary clients.

text.text: Two examples of genderinclusive approaches are meta-therapy 3 and Hirsch's Acoustic Assumptions. 4
text.formatted: Two examples of genderinclusive approaches are meta-therapy 3 and Hirsch's Acoustic Assumptions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref>

text.text: Meta-therapy 3 uses purposeful dialogue to shape clients' understanding of therapy and support awareness, self-efficacy, and skill acquisition throughout GAVT.

Meta-therapeutic conversations target clients' "cognitions, knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and/or awareness to perform volitional behaviors" in voice therapy. 19 (p. 9) While the exact definition of meta-therapy continues to evolve, 20 the five self-referential goals of meta-therapy 19(p. 5) are: 1.
text.formatted: Meta-therapeutic conversations target clients' "cognitions, knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and/or awareness to perform volitional behaviors" in voice therapy. <ref type="bibr">19 (p. 9)</ref> While the exact definition of meta-therapy continues to evolve, <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">20</ref> the five self-referential goals of meta-therapy <ref type="bibr">19(p. 5)</ref> are: 1.

text.text: The process of vocal improvement (i.e., progress is not necessarily linear); 2.
The patient's role in treatment (i.e., active participation); 3.
The role of self-efficacy (e.g., perceived control of respiration or voice); 4.
How the relationship between voice and identity can affect treatment (e.g., new voice may feel incompatible with their sense of self); and 5.
How affective states influence treatment (e.g., recognizing and navigating stress-related vocal changes).
Meta-therapeutic conversations can illuminate the facilitators and barriers involved in GAVT skill-building.

Gathering insight into the client's lived experiences can inform intervention design for optimal GAVT experiences and outcomes. 3, 19 This approach can help establish GAVT goals, providing a structured framework clinicians can use to guide clients toward their desired voice and communication style. 4 conceptualize several speech characteristics along continua extending from perceptually "brighter" to perceptually "darker" speech qualities.
text.formatted: Gathering insight into the client's lived experiences can inform intervention design for optimal GAVT experiences and outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">19</ref> This approach can help establish GAVT goals, providing a structured framework clinicians can use to guide clients toward their desired voice and communication style. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> conceptualize several speech characteristics along continua extending from perceptually "brighter" to perceptually "darker" speech qualities.

text.text: Following this approach, clients modify their voicing, articulatory contact pressure, vowel shape, and utterance finish to produce their desired voice and communication style.

The eight steps of Hirsch's Acoustic Assumptions are listed in the original publication as "Instructional Steps for Using the Acoustic Assumptions." 4(p. 77-78) First, clinicians review relevant anatomy and physiology and co-create a coding system (e.g., for marking therapeutic stimuli) that cues clients to make specific voice and communication changes.
text.formatted: The eight steps of Hirsch's Acoustic Assumptions are listed in the original publication as "Instructional Steps for Using the Acoustic Assumptions." <ref type="bibr">4(p. 77-78)</ref> First, clinicians review relevant anatomy and physiology and co-create a coding system (e.g., for marking therapeutic stimuli) that cues clients to make specific voice and communication changes.

text.text: Using functional stimuli, clients begin with shorter, simpler utterances (i.e., 4-6 words), then progress to longer, more complex utterances (i.e., a "programmatic approach" 21(p. 2) ).
text.formatted: Using functional stimuli, clients begin with shorter, simpler utterances (i.e., 4-6 words), then progress to longer, more complex utterances (i.e., a "programmatic approach" <ref type="bibr">21(p. 2)</ref> ).

text.text: Hirsch recommends training clients to identify potential acoustic challenges in an utterance (e.g., the /u/ vowel in "How are you?"), identifying potential solutions (e.g., using an /i/ shape when producing "you" for a brighter sound), and silently practicing skill use (e.g., silently mouthing "How are you?"
with the /i/shaped vowel for "you" for a brighter sound).

Finally, clients speak the utterance aloud, taking multiple trials to practice implementing and refining their skill use with the utterance. 4 The AA offer an inherently customizable approach to GAVT in that the specified gestures may be combined (i.e., mixed and matched) to create a variety of voice and communication characteristics across the spectrum of human gender expression.
text.formatted: Finally, clients speak the utterance aloud, taking multiple trials to practice implementing and refining their skill use with the utterance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> The AA offer an inherently customizable approach to GAVT in that the specified gestures may be combined (i.e., mixed and matched) to create a variety of voice and communication characteristics across the spectrum of human gender expression.

text.text: For example, combining an /i/ vowel shape, greater articulatory contact pressure, and a closed finish may yield both darker and perceptually feminine characteristics. 4, 21 While the original article 4 describes binary applications of the AA and outcomes for GAVT, subsequent findings 21 include use cases for nonbinary clients.
text.formatted: For example, combining an /i/ vowel shape, greater articulatory contact pressure, and a closed finish may yield both darker and perceptually feminine characteristics. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">21</ref> While the original article <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> describes binary applications of the AA and outcomes for GAVT, subsequent findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">21</ref> include use cases for nonbinary clients.

text.text: With repetition and clinical guidance, trained skills can become more automatic and intuitive over time. 4, 22 Preliminary research suggests that AA approaches support GAVT goals with improvements in acoustic measures, listener perceptions, and self-reports of voice-related well-being. 21, 23 Thus far, research has primarily focused on feminizing goals, and emerging research supports using AA to target feminizing goals. 21, 23 However, the AA remain inclusive of nonbinary clients because they allow clients to select combinations of voice and communication characteristics to create an individualized voice and communication style, 4, 21 thereby accommodating a broad array of GAVT goals.
text.formatted: With repetition and clinical guidance, trained skills can become more automatic and intuitive over time. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">22</ref> Preliminary research suggests that AA approaches support GAVT goals with improvements in acoustic measures, listener perceptions, and self-reports of voice-related well-being. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">23</ref> Thus far, research has primarily focused on feminizing goals, and emerging research supports using AA to target feminizing goals. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">23</ref> However, the AA remain inclusive of nonbinary clients because they allow clients to select combinations of voice and communication characteristics to create an individualized voice and communication style, <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">21</ref> thereby accommodating a broad array of GAVT goals.

text.text: At present, GAVT interventions investigated and validated in research studies are predominantly tied to binary perceptions and outcomes, which may or may not reflect an individual's gender identity.

Nonbinary individuals have distinct lived experiences from other groups within the TGD community (e.g., transgender women, transgender men), therefore their GAVT goals may exceed the scope of binary-adherent targets.
Clinicians remain obligated to deliver evidence-based interventions to the fullest extent possible.

Well-established acoustic theories of human speech production, such as source-filter theory, 15 provide theoretical support for genderinclusive approaches in areas where the empirical literature is still developing.
text.formatted: Well-established acoustic theories of human speech production, such as source-filter theory, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">15</ref> provide theoretical support for genderinclusive approaches in areas where the empirical literature is still developing.

text.text: In summary, GAVT approaches must be sufficiently broad enough to cover the wide variety of GAVT goals for the TGD community.
Gender-inclusive approaches, such as meta-therapy 3 and the AA 4 are inherently customizable interventions for GAVT.
Future research should prioritize outcome measures explicitly reflecting the lived experiences and GAVT goals of nonbinary individuals.
Leveraging more gender-inclusive approaches may enable clinicians to more comprehensively support nonbinary clients in GAVT.
